summary:
San Martín is a department of Peru. Neither source in the inventory contains San Martín-specific content, so the department carries no provision of its own and is assessed against the national framework as it stands across Peru.

The national framework is the operative one for a trans visitor. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

In February 2025 the Comisión de Mujer y Familia of the Congress approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex. The text carries narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where entry is required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. At that stage it still required plenary backing. Its reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, and that the measure is discriminatory.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes, enacted in April 2025, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The same legislative package mandates that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their gender identity, and bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity". The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. IDEHPUCP also documented dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the April 2025 provision does not meet on IDEHPUCP's reading.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

Legal gender recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation. That gap is what makes the DNI check the practical enforcement mechanism for the restroom restriction.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected; its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained by the same package. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The two bathroom bills were approved at committee level in February 2025 and enacted through the April 2025 children's and adolescents' statute, so a visitor encounters one operative rule rather than competing ones. The provision's origin in a 2023 signage complaint at the capital's airport suggests the dispute is triggered by visible markers, not by conduct, which raises the exposure of any trans visitor whose presentation or documents do not align.

Enforcement is expected to rest on security staff rather than on police powers, placing discretion in the hands of gym receptionists, venue staff and guards who have no duty to assess a person's gender identity and every incentive to apply the DNI literally. The INDECOPI outcome in the SmartFit complaint shows a consumer body declining to intervene against that practice.

The national position sits in open conflict with the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 and with the regional human-rights convention, and the IDEHPUCP analysis states the constitutional breach plainly. The December 2025 sentence in the Azul Rojas Marín case, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, shows the regional mechanism remains available where domestic remedies fail, but it took close to two decades.

Peru's 2017 removal of LGBT hate-crime coverage places it alongside Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American countries without it, so a trans visitor has no hate-crime shield of the kind common elsewhere on the continent.
localsOnly:
Residents of San Martín live under the same national rules as visitors: Article 5.1 of the April 2025 statute governs restroom access by birth sex, and the ban on inclusive signage removes "women in their diversity" and similar wording from venues across the department.

Legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive for residents, which means the mismatch between documents and presentation is a standing condition of daily life rather than a travel anomaly, and the DNI check applies to residents every time they use a monitored facility.

In June 2024 health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, which changes how trans patients are described in clinical settings; IDEHPUCP's documentation of the restroom provision and of congressional rhetoric provides a domestic reference point for complaints.

The December 2025 conviction of three police officers to 17 years for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín is a domestic sentence and sets the first precedent in Peru for a crime motivated by sexual discrimination. The July 2025 ruling by a Lima constitutional court against an anti-equality decree is likewise available to residents as domestic authority.

No San Martín-specific enforcement record, departmental violence tally, or local administrative instruction on restroom access appears in the sources; residents and visitors are treated alike under the national rule.
outOfScopeNotes:
Neither source carries San Martín-specific content, so the department's on-the-ground application of the restroom statute, any local government or business guidance, and any departmental violence figures remain not sourced here.

That enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI is Gianna Camacho's stated expectation as quoted in February 2025, not a documented enforcement practice recorded for San Martín or elsewhere; whether venues in the department in fact apply a document check is unresolved.

The February 2025 dictamen is described in that article as still requiring plenary backing, while the April 2025 analysis records plenary approval on 2 April 2025 and promulgation of the statute; the two accounts are read as sequential stages of the same package, and the exact entry into force of each article is not stated in the inventory.

Whether the narrow exceptions written into the February text (custody, accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, medical need) survived into the enacted Article 5.1 verbatim is not confirmed by the sources, and the phrase "biological sex" in the parent framework is not quoted from Article 5.1 itself.

Statistics on killings and hate crimes are national and, on the source's own account, a sub-registry; no breakdown by department is available, and there is no sourcing for reporting rates or police responsiveness in San Martín.
